{{short description|Generalization of open map in topology}}
In [[topology]], a branch of mathematics, a '''quasi-open map''' (also called '''quasi-interior map''') is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] that generalizes the notion of [[open map]].

== Definition ==

A function <math>f:X\to Y</math> between [[topological space]]s is called '''quasi-open''' if, for any nonempty [[open set]] <math>U\subseteq X</math>, the [[interior (topology)|interior]] of <math>f(U)</math> in <math>Y</math> is nonempty.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mardešić |first1=Sibe |last2=Papić |first2=Pavle |title=Continuous images of ordered compacta, the Suslin property and dyadic compacta |journal=Period. Math.-Phys. Astron., II. Ser. |date=1962 |volume=17 |pages=3-22 |url=https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/glasnik/skenirano/mardesicpapic1962.pdf |zbl=0119.17906}}Definition 3 on page 7</ref><ref name="Kao">{{cite journal |last1=Kao |first1=Kuo Shih |title=A note on M1-spaces |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics |date=1983 |volume=108 |issue=1 |pages=121–128 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1983.108.121 |zbl=0487.54029}}</ref>
Such a function has also been called a '''quasi-interior map'''.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=A.|last1=Blokh|first2=L.|last2=Oversteegen|first3=E.D.|last3=Tymchatyn|title=On almost one-to-one maps|journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=2006|doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-06-03922-5|volume=358|issue=11 |pages=5003–5015|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Properties ==

Let <math>f:X\to Y</math> be a map between [[topological spaces]].
* If <math>f</math> is continuous, it need not be quasi-open.  For example, the constant map <math>f:\R\to\R</math> defined by <math>f(x)=0</math> is continuous but not quasi-open.
* Conversely, if <math>f</math> is quasi-open, it need not be continuous.  For example, the map <math>f:\R\to\R</math> defined by <math>f(x)=x</math> if <math>x<0</math> and <math>f(x)=x+1</math> if <math>x\ge 0</math> is quasi-open but not continuous.
* If <math>f</math> is [[open function|open]], then <math>f</math> is quasi-open.<ref name="Kao" />  The converse is not true in general.  For example, the continuous function <math>f:\R\to\R,x\mapsto\sin(x)</math> is quasi-open but not open.
* If <math>f</math> is a [[local homeomorphism]], then <math>f</math> is quasi-open.<ref name="Kim">{{cite journal|title=A Note on Quasi-Open Maps|first=Jae Woon|last=Kim|journal=Journal of the Korean Mathematical Society|series=B: The Pure and Applied Mathematics|volume=5|number=1|pages=1–3|year=1998|url=http://icms.kaist.ac.kr/mathnet/kms_tex/50115.pdf|access-date=October 20, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304051743/http://icms.kaist.ac.kr/mathnet/kms_tex/50115.pdf|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* The composition of two quasi-open maps is quasi-open.<ref group=note> This means that if <math>f:X\to Y</math> and <math>g:Y\to Z</math> are both quasi-open, then the function composition <math>g\circ f: X\to Z</math> is quasi-open.</ref><ref name="Kao" />
